legend: Hacker Kirill decided to develop a new random number generator. To do this, he took two large numbers n%%ZSMJ0%% and m%%ZSMJ1%%, turned them into powers of two, added them up, and raised the resulting amount to a small power of k%%ZSMJ2%%, and got some number r=(2n+2m)k%%ZSMJ3%%. Random numbers were supposed to be cut from the binary notation of the number r%%ZSMJ4%%.

When Kirill posted his ideas on the forum, one of his colleagues said that the numbers obtained would be too non-random, pointing out that even just the number of ones in the binary representation in the number r%%ZSMJ5%% is too predictable.

Help Kirill verify his colleague's statement. Write a program that uses the numbers n%%ZSMJ6%%, m%%ZSMJ7%% and k%%ZSMJ8%% to determine the number of ones in the binary representation of the number r=(2n+2m)k%%ZSMJ9%%.
input: The single line contains 3 integers n(0≤n≤109)%%ZSMJ10%%, m(0≤m≤109)%%ZSMJ11%% and k(0≤k≤100)%%ZSMJ12%%, separated by a space.
output: In a single line, print a number – the amount of ones in the binary representation of the number r=(2n+2m)k%%ZSMJ13%%.
